analysis.one_liner: Permanently eliminates all federal tax on capital gains for individuals and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently eliminate the capital gains tax was introduced in April 2008 with 33 Republican cosponsors, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it and it died at the end of the 110th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set the federal tax rate on capital gains — the profits from selling stocks, real estate, and other investments — to zero percent, permanently, for both individuals and corporations. It would also apply the zero rate to the alternative minimum tax and erase the scheduled end of the 2003 capital gains rate cuts [S2] [S3]. Capital gains income goes mostly to the wealthiest households and to corporations, so the bill would sharply cut what they pay while reducing federal revenue that other taxpayers or future spending would have to cover. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment portfolios and corporations that realize capital gains. Capital gains income is heavily concentrated among the wealthiest Americans, so a permanent zero rate would primarily cut taxes for high-income investors and profitable corporations [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It sets the individual capital gains rate to 0 percent, replacing the rate structure created by the 2003 tax law (which had cut the top capital gains rate to 15 percent), and it repeals that law's expiration date of December 31, 2008, making the zero rate permanent [S2] [S3].
It applies the zero rate for the alternative minimum tax as well as the regular income tax, so investors could not be pushed back into paying tax on gains through the AMT [S2] [S3].

It rewrites the corporate capital gains provision so that a corporation's net capital gain is taxed at 0 percent instead of the regular corporate rate, and makes related technical changes to withholding rules on dispositions and distributions [S3].
The change takes effect for taxable years ending after enactment, so it would apply immediately rather than phasing in [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost — every dollar of capital gains income currently taxed at 15 percent or the corporate rate would become untaxed. Whatever replaces that revenue, or the debt from forgoing it, falls on other taxpayers and future budgets [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Other taxpayers and the federal budget

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates all federal tax on capital gains for both individuals and corporations, permanently and with no offsetting revenue provision anywhere in its text [S3]. Because capital gains income flows overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, the cost of the tax cut would be concentrated at the top while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers, by borrowing, or by future spending cuts.

The CRS summary confirms the bill also removes the scheduled December 31, 2008 expiration of the reduced individual capital gains rates from the 2003 tax law, converting a temporary rate cut into a permanent one rather than letting it lapse on schedule [S2].
Making the rate permanent applies it for all future years, so the fiscal cost compounds over time instead of ending with the 2008 sunset the 2003 law had built in [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows almost entirely to households and corporations with large capital gains — the top of the income distribution — while the cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue that someone else must eventually cover through taxes, borrowing, or reduced services. The bill contains no mechanism to pay for itself and no provision aimed at working people, so the trade it offers ordinary taxpayers is straightforward: they give up the revenue, and the gains go to asset holders.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 with no vote ever held.

narrative.text: Rep. Wally Herger introduced the bill on April 24, 2008, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the House never voted, and the bill's only actions are its introduction and referral [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill expired without a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers as a whole are better off, because the bill would have permanently zeroed out taxes on capital gains income that flows overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households and corporations, with no way to pay for the lost revenue. It cost its supporters nothing, since it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers; the bill never advanced

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 24, 2008 and took no further action on it — no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor [S1] [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, and a permanent 0 percent rate on gains — including under the AMT — would eliminate their main tax liability on investment sales entirely [S2] [S3].

The bill taxes corporate net capital gains at 0 percent in place of regular corporate rates and cuts withholding-related rates to zero, directly reducing the tax burden on corporate investment income [S3].
A zero rate on gains raises the after-tax return on selling appreciated assets, encouraging more realizations and investment activity that funds and brokers are paid to handle [S3].
